Strike the centre or the edge of the head with the palm or a stick; different positions give different timbres. The force of the stroke sets the volume. It sounds by being struck, so watch the striking position and the control of force.

The repinique is a double-headed membranophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 211.212.11, usually built with a tubular metal shell, nylon heads and metal tuning rods, without snares, and hung from a shoulder strap. It is tuned very high, leads or solos in the samba percussion ensemble, and sets the tempo for the other parts; the Rio style is played with one hand and one wooden stick, Bahia mostly with two sticks. The musical director calls the rhythmic changes, helping the dancers keep the samba rhythm, and it is common in the samba percussion ensembles of the Rio and São Paulo carnival and of Bahia. It also appears in American classical music.
雷皮尼克鼓源自巴西，是森巴文化中不可或缺的打擊樂器。其起源可追溯至巴西非洲裔社群: The repinique comes from Brazil and is an indispensable percussion instrument of samba culture. Its origins can be traced to the meeting of Afro-Brazilian communities with local musical traditions, and it matured above all in the carnival celebrations of Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo. The instrument combines African drumming traditions with the character of Brazilian samba music, taking shape over decades of change. As samba culture spread through Brazil, the repinique was gradually taken into the percussion band, and in Bahia there is a local variant called the repique. Its distinctively high tuning lets it cut through a large percussion band, and it has become an irreplaceable lead instrument. Today the instrument is a symbol of Brazilian carnival and samba music, and it has won recognition on the international stage.
雷皮尼克鼓為雙面膜鳴鼓，編號 211.212.11。來源指出其調音很高，產生能穿: The repinique is a double-headed membranophone, number 211.212.11. The source notes that it is tuned high, producing a timbre that cuts through the other parts of a samba bateria, and that it is used to lead and to solo. The shell is usually metal, with nylon heads tensioned by metal tuning rods; compared with the Brazilian caixa it is smaller in diameter, taller and has no snares. The source mentions no specific range and no means of volume control.
